passages.original: 10. Quod si quis, c ut Marcion et Manichæus, reprehendendum Dei putat esse judicium, quia vel oraculum de circumcisione celebranda edendum putavit esse, vel legem qua sanguinis effusio mandatur; necesse est ut is cnam Dominum Jcsum reprehendendum arbitretur , qui nou exiguum, sed mullum sanguinem pro hujus mundi effudit redemptione, et hodieque nos fundere jubet sanguinem nostrum pro tanto religionis certamine, dicens: Qui vult me sequi, tollat crucem suam, et sequatur me (Matth.
passages.english: 10. But if anyone, like Marcion and Manichaeus, thinks that the judgment of God is to be faulted, because he thought fit to issue either an oracle about the celebration of circumcision, or a law by which the shedding of blood is commanded, then he must necessarily think that the Lord Jesus too is to be faulted, who shed not a little but much blood for the redemption of this world, and even today commands us to shed our own blood in so great a contest of religion, saying: "Whoever wishes to follow me, let him take up his cross and follow me" (Matt.
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected: 'cnam' read as 'etiam', 'Jcsum' as 'Jesum', 'nou' as 'non', 'mullum' as 'multum'; the stray 'c' before 'ut Marcion' is taken as a footnote mark. 'Manichaeus' is Mani, founder of Manichaeism. The citation continues in the following text (Matt. 16:24).

passages.original: Laudat Polybium, cuju rogatu te binas ad Segatium et Delphinum epistola. scripsisse significat.
passages.english: He praises Polybius, at whose request he indicates that he wrote two letters to Segatius and Delphinus.
passages.notes: This is an editorial summary (argumentum) of the letter, not Ambrose's own text. Scanning errors: 'cuju' read as 'cujus'; 'te binas' read as 'se binas'; 'epistola.' read as 'epistolas'.
